code.overview: Detect and Emit are fully code: the tools/linter-setup CLI (run, detect.ts, emit.ts, hash.ts, deps.ts, registry.ts) with templates in lib/linters/. Asking the user, merging a sidecar into an existing config, tuning and committing are all done by the agent from the skill text; the CLI never edits an existing config and has no merge or tune command.

refs.anchor: export function detect(repoPath: string, srcRoot = DEFAULT_SRC_ROOT): DetectResult[] {
refs.title: detect: which languages does the repo use?
refs.explain: It lists the files git tracks and skips the linter templates and setup tool themselves. Each remaining file extension is looked up in the registry to get a language. A tsconfig.json adds TypeScript even with no .ts files, and when TypeScript is present plain JS is dropped because both would write the same ESLint config.
refs.why: This is the first half of the Detect stage. The skip list stops scaffold from detecting its own sample configs as languages in use.

refs.anchor: const configPath = entry.configFile ? join(repoPath, entry.configFile) : null;
refs.title: detect: give each language one of four states
refs.explain: For each language it looks for the config file named in the registry. No file means none. A file without the scaffold marker line means foreign. With a marker, it compares the hash stamped on that line to the hash of the current template: equal, unstamped or uncomputable means scaffold, and a different hash means stale.
refs.why: These four states decide what the skill offers: fresh add, merge, re-merge or skip. Treating an unknown hash as current avoids nagging about a config that may be fine.

refs.title: templateHash: the stamp that marks staleness
refs.explain: It finds the language's template config under lib/linters/. It returns the first 12 hex characters of the sha256 of that file. It returns null when the language has no config file or the template cannot be found.
refs.why: Detect compares this value with the one stamped in the repo's config. It tracks the template, not the user's edits, so tuning a config never makes it stale.

refs.title: run --detect-only: print the states as JSON
refs.explain: When the --detect-only flag is present, the CLI runs detect on the target path and prints the list of language and state pairs as JSON. It then returns without reading stdin or writing any file.
refs.why: This is the exact command Step 1 runs. The agent parses this JSON and stops when every state is scaffold.

refs.anchor: // Suggest /add-linter for any detected language not yet using scaffold thresholds
refs.title: sync: the hint that sends users to /add-linter
refs.explain: After a real sync (not a dry run) it runs the same detect function on the repo. If any language is not in the scaffold state it prints a hint naming those languages and says to run /add-linter. If detect throws, for example outside a git repo, the hint is skipped.
refs.why: This is the second way the flow starts. It reuses detect, so the hint and the skill always agree on what needs action.

refs.title: run: read the confirmed list and emit each language
refs.explain: Without --detect-only the CLI reads stdin and exits with an error if it is empty or not a JSON array. It then calls emit once per language in the list, and exits with an error if any emit throws.
refs.why: This is the hand-off from Ask to Emit: only languages the user confirmed are in the list. The CLI itself does not ask anyone anything.

refs.title: emit: write, skip, or write a sidecar
refs.explain: For the config, the workflow and any extra files, it finds the template and the destination. If the destination exists and already has the scaffold marker, it is skipped. If it exists without the marker, the template is written beside it as <file>.scaffold-new and the original is not touched. If nothing is there, the file is written; a new Prettier config also becomes a sidecar when the repo already has another Prettier setup.
refs.why: This is the rule that the CLI never edits an existing config. Without the sidecar branch, a user's own lint rules would be overwritten.

refs.anchor: // Stamp the template hash into the config's marker line, so detection can later
refs.title: stampMarker: put the template hash on the marker line
refs.explain: When a config is written, the first occurrence of the marker comment is replaced with the marker followed by sha256: and the template hash. Workflows and extra files are copied without a stamp.
refs.why: Detect later reads this stamp to tell a current scaffold config from a stale one. The Merge step must carry this line over by hand for the same reason.

refs.anchor: const deps: MergeResult = adopted ? mergeDevDependencies(targetRepo, language) : { added: [], status: 'sidecar' };
refs.title: emit: add packages and scripts only when the config is adopted
refs.explain: A config counts as adopted when the language has one and it did not end up as a sidecar. Only then does emit call the two package.json merges for devDependencies and scripts. For a sidecar both results are returned with status sidecar and nothing is added.
refs.why: This keeps packages out of package.json until the user has actually taken the config. The agent adds them later when it applies a merge.

refs.anchor: function mergeInto(targetRepo: string, section: Section, entries: Record<string, string>): MergeResult {
refs.title: mergeInto: add missing package.json entries, change nothing else
refs.explain: It returns early if there is nothing to add, no package.json, or the file does not parse. It collects the names already present (for packages, in both dependencies and devDependencies). Each missing name is appended; present names are left as they are. If anything was added, the file is rewritten with its original indentation and trailing newline.
refs.why: This is why running the CLI twice is safe and why an existing version or lint script is never changed.

refs.anchor: // package.json scripts added on adopt. Type-aware autofix can rewrite code
refs.title: registry: the TypeScript lint scripts
refs.explain: The registry entry for TypeScript lists the scripts added on adopt: lint, format:check, format and lint:fix. lint:fix runs the ESLint autofix and then tsc --noEmit.
refs.why: The skill forbids a bare autofix on a type-aware config. Shipping the type-check inside the script makes the safe form the default.

refs.anchor: for (const f of result.skipped)   console.log(`  skipped   ${lang}  ${f}  (scaffold already present)`);
refs.title: run: one result line per file
refs.explain: After each emit the CLI prints a line for every written file, every sidecar (marked original unchanged) and every skipped file. It prints the packages it added with a reminder to run npm install, or the npm i -D command to run by hand when there is no package.json. Added scripts are not printed.
refs.why: The agent builds its Step 6 report from these lines. The merged, tuned and declined rows of that report have no CLI output and come from the agent.

refs.title: Test: an existing config is left alone
refs.explain: The test writes its own eslint.config.mjs into a temporary repo and runs emit for JS. It then checks the file is byte-for-byte unchanged and that eslint.config.mjs.scaffold-new now exists beside it.
refs.why: It pins the promise the Merge stage depends on: the original and the sidecar both exist for the agent to compare.

promptOnly.what: The agent asks one multi-select question covering every language with state none, foreign or stale, and stops if the user confirms none.

The agent reads the config and its .scaffold-new sidecar, proposes a merge that keeps the user's values and the stamped marker line, shows the diff and conflicts, and on approval backs up to .bak, writes and removes the sidecar.

The agent proposes tuning values from the repo's code, reports per language, and offers the commit while leaving out .bak and .scaffold-new files; nothing in the repo blocks those files from being committed.
